posts.title: The after-hours audit
posts.hook: Call your own business at 6:15 tonight.
posts.kicker: Count the rings. That is the leak.
posts.caption:
The first thing I do with every new client is call their business after hours. Not to catch anyone. To hear what their customers hear.

Usually it is six rings, a full voicemail box, or a greeting recorded in 2019. Nobody inside the business ever hears it, because nobody calls their own line at dinner.

Do it tonight. Call from a number your team does not know, ask a real question, and write down how long it takes to get an answer.

If the answer is "tomorrow morning," that is the job for your first voice agent: it picks up on ring one, answers the question, books the visit, and texts you the summary. You still own every customer. You just stop losing the ones who call at 6:15.

Save this and run the audit before Friday.

posts.title: Four things you should always own
posts.hook: Rent the tools. Own the asset.
posts.kicker: If your agency vanished tomorrow, would you still run?
posts.caption:
I have taken over a lot of projects where the owner did not own their own business online.

The domain was registered to a former web guy. The phone number lived in a vendor account they could not log into. The customer list was locked in software that charged extra to export it.

That is not a tech problem. It is a leverage problem, and you are on the wrong side of it.

Everything I build, the client owns. The domain in their name. The code in their account. The logins handed over with a written guide on how to run it. If they never call me again, the business keeps working.

Check your four today: domain, customer list, phone number, website logins. If any of them is in someone else's name, fix that first.

posts.title: Set up a Claude Project for your business
posts.hook: Build your business a brain once.
posts.kicker: Then every chat already knows who you are.
posts.caption:
If you open a blank AI chat every time and explain your business from scratch, you are doing the setup work over and over.

Do it once. In Claude, create a Project for your business and load it up: your services, your service area, your best reviews, a few emails that sound exactly like you. Then write the project instructions like a note to a new hire: how you talk, what you never promise, words you hate.

Now every chat you start in that Project already knows you. Ask for a review reply, a Facebook post, a quote follow-up, and it comes back in your voice on the first try.

Thirty minutes of setup. It pays you back every single day after.

posts.title: The lead response rule
posts.hook: Five minutes, or the lead is cold.
posts.kicker: The clock starts the second they reach out.
posts.caption:
Five minutes versus thirty. That is the difference the MIT lead response study measured: 21 times more likely to qualify when you get back within five.

Nobody is getting back within five. Not because they do not care, but because they are on a roof, in a meeting, or at their kid's game.

That is exactly the gap an agent fills. The form comes in, and within a minute the customer gets a text that sounds like you: "Got it! Is this for the front yard or the whole property?" One question. Now they are in a conversation with you instead of filling out the next company's form.

You still close the job. The agent just keeps the door open until you can walk through it.

posts.title: Turn your process into a Claude Skill
posts.hook: Teach Claude a skill once. Use it forever.
posts.kicker: Your best way of doing something, saved.
posts.caption:
Here is the difference between using AI and building with it.

Using it: you type a prompt, get something okay, fix it, and do it all again tomorrow.

Building with it: you write down how you want something done once. Your review reply style. Your rules for a quote follow-up. Two examples you love and three things never to say. Then you save it as a Skill in Claude.

Now every time that task comes up, Claude follows your rules. Your office manager gets the result you would. Your new hire does too.

That is how a one-person shop starts operating like a team without adding payroll. Your judgment, written down once, working every day.

posts.title: Why your voice agent feels fake
posts.hook: On the phone, speed beats smart.
posts.kicker: A pause is what makes an agent sound like a robot.
posts.caption:
Trade secret most agencies will not tell you: the thing that makes a voice agent sound fake is almost never the voice.

It is the pause.

People answer each other in about a fifth of a second. When an agent takes two full seconds to respond, the caller's brain files it as "machine" before it says a word. You can have the smartest script in the world and still lose them in that silence.

So when I tune an agent, speed comes first. A fast model handles the live conversation. The slower, smarter work (writing the job notes, updating your calendar, texting you the summary) happens after the caller hangs up.

Short answers, fast turns, heavy lifting later. That is the whole trick.

posts.title: Mine your reviews for headlines
posts.hook: Your customers already wrote your ads.
posts.kicker: They are sitting in your reviews.
posts.caption:
You describe your business with your words. Customers buy with theirs.

Here is a ten minute exercise that rewrites homepages. Copy your reviews into Claude and ask it to pull the exact phrases customers use, grouped by theme.

You will see things like "showed up when they said they would" and "didn't make me feel dumb for asking." Those are your headlines. Nobody searches for "quality craftsmanship." They search for someone who shows up.

Then ask what they were worried about before they hired you. That worry is what your ad should answer first.

Your best copywriters already work for free. They are your happy customers.

posts.title: Why AI agents go sideways
posts.hook: One agent. One job.
posts.kicker: The agent that does everything does everything badly.
posts.caption:
The most common mistake I see: one giant AI that is supposed to answer calls, write quotes, schedule crews, chase invoices and post on Instagram.

It will do all of that. Badly.

Agents are like employees. The receptionist is not also your bookkeeper. Give each agent one job, a short rulebook, and a clear definition of done. The phone agent's job is done when the visit is booked and you have the summary. That is it.

This is also how you keep control. When the follow-up texts sound off, you open one rulebook and fix one thing. Nothing else changes.

Small, focused, boring agents are the ones that quietly work every single day.

posts.title: The one job, ten posts prompt
posts.hook: One finished job is ten pieces of marketing.
posts.kicker: Most businesses post it once, or not at all.
posts.caption:
Every job you finish is a story, a photo set, and proof you can do the work. Most of it disappears into your camera roll.

Here is the fix. When a job wraps, drop three photos and a few notes into Claude. "Kitchen backsplash in Whitefish, customer was nervous about grout color, we did samples on a board first, she teared up when she saw it."

Then ask for everything at once: a Facebook post, a Google profile update, a before-and-after caption, a two-line email to past customers, and a FAQ answer for your site about choosing grout color.

Claude reads the photos, so it describes the actual work. You approve, you schedule, and one Tuesday job just filled a week.

posts.title: How AI picks who to recommend
posts.hook: Ask ChatGPT who the best in your trade is, in your town.
posts.kicker: If the answer is not you, here is why.
posts.caption:
Try this right now. Open ChatGPT and ask: "Who is the best [your trade] in [your town]?"

Screenshot the answer. That is the new word of mouth.

More of your customers are asking an AI instead of scrolling Google, and the AI is not guessing. It is reading. Your reviews, your directory listings, your own website.

The businesses that show up have a few things in common. Their site says exactly what they do and where, in plain sentences. Their name and number match everywhere. And their pages answer real questions, like "how long does a roof replacement take" or "do you haul appliances."

A gorgeous site with no words on it is invisible to a machine that reads. Write for the reader that recommends you.

posts.title: The skeptic prompt
posts.hook: Make Claude your toughest customer.
posts.kicker: Let it tear the offer apart before a real buyer does.
posts.caption:
AI is too nice by default. Ask it if your ad is good and it will tell you it is great.

So do not ask that. Give it a job instead: "You are a busy homeowner who got burned by the last company you hired. Read this and tell me every reason you would not call. Rank them."

Now you get the truth. The price is hidden. It is not clear what area you serve. There is no proof you have done this exact job before. The button says "Learn More" and nobody wants to learn more, they want a quote.

Fix the top three objections and run it again. It is the cheapest focus group you will ever hold, and it is open at midnight.

posts.title: The quote follow-up that closes
posts.hook: The money is in the second text.
posts.kicker: Most quotes do not lose. They just go quiet.
posts.caption:
You send the quote. Silence. You assume they went with someone cheaper.

Most of the time they did not. They got busy. The quote is sitting under forty other emails, and the first company that follows up gets the job.

Here is the follow-up I build for clients:

Day 1: the quote, plus one question.
Day 3: something genuinely useful about their project. Not "just checking in."
Day 7: a simple, friendly schedule question.

Three touches, written in your voice, sent by an agent that stops the second the customer replies and hands the conversation straight back to you.

Nobody on your team has time to track every open quote. An agent does not forget.

posts.title: Give Codex your website to-do list
posts.hook: Codex can fix your website while you make dinner.
posts.kicker: If you own the code, you can hand it the chores.
posts.caption:
This is the part of AI nobody is telling small business owners about.

OpenAI's Codex is a coding agent. Point it at your website's code, give it a task in plain English, and it does the work and hands you the change to approve. "Add our winter hours to the footer." "Add a page for gutter cleaning." "Make the phone number tap to call on mobile."

The catch: you have to own your code. If your site lives in a builder you rent, or with an agency that holds the keys, there is nothing to hand Codex.

That is why every site I build lives in the client's own account. Owning it is what lets you keep improving it without asking permission, from me or anyone else.

posts.title: The voice memo method
posts.hook: Your best AI prompt is a 10-minute voice memo.
posts.kicker: Train an agent the way you train a new hire.
posts.caption:
You do not need to learn prompt engineering. You need to talk.

Every good agent I build starts the same way: the owner records a voice memo explaining how they handle a call, a quote, or a complaint. Driving, walking the dog, sitting on the tailgate. Ten minutes, no script.

That recording holds the stuff no template has. The regular who always gets a callback from you personally. The job you never take in January. The way you actually say no.

Transcribe it, add your top five customer questions, then write the "never do this" list. Never quote a price over the phone. Never promise a date. Never argue.

That is a real instruction set, in your voice, built from how your business actually runs.

posts.title: The windshield content method
posts.hook: Talk your marketing on the drive home.
posts.kicker: You are better out loud than at a keyboard.
posts.caption:
Most owners I work with are great at explaining their work. Out loud. Put them in front of a blank page and they freeze.

So skip the blank page. On the drive home, talk. Use Claude's voice mode or a plain voice memo, and answer one question: what did a customer ask you today, and what did you tell them?

"Lady asked me today if she really needs to seal her deck every year. Honestly, depends on the sun..." That is a post. A better post than anything you would type at 9pm.

Hand it to Claude and ask it to keep your phrases and cut the rambling. That is it. Your commute just became your content team.

posts.title: The stress test before launch
posts.hook: Test your agent like a customer on their worst day.
posts.kicker: The polite demo call proves nothing.
posts.caption:
Every AI agent sounds amazing in a quiet office with a polite caller. That is not your customer.

Your customer is calling from a job site. Their kid is yelling in the back seat. Their name is spelled with a silent letter and their address has a unit number.

Before anything I build goes live, I call it like that. From my truck, windows down. I interrupt it. I change my mind. I ask it something it has no business answering.

If it keeps up, spells the name back right, and hands me to a human when it should, it ships. If it does not, it does not.

Ask whoever builds your agent to show you the worst call they tested. If they only have the nice one, keep testing.

posts.title: The competitor teardown
posts.hook: Screenshot your top three competitors.
posts.kicker: Then let Claude show you where you win.
posts.caption:
You know who you lose jobs to. You probably have not looked at their websites side by side with yours in a while.

Claude can read screenshots. Grab the homepages of your top three competitors plus your own, drop all four in, and ask it to compare them the way a customer would.

It spots things fast. One promises a response within an hour. One shows prices. One has 200 reviews on the homepage while yours are buried on a separate page. And sometimes it tells you your site says something better than all three, you just said it too far down.

This is not about copying anyone. It is about knowing exactly what a customer sees when they are comparing you.

posts.title: Where the time actually goes
posts.hook: Stop automating tasks. Automate the handoff.
posts.kicker: Deals do not die in the work. They die in the wait.
posts.caption:
When operators ask me what to automate first, they usually point at a task. Writing quotes. Scheduling. Invoicing.

Those are rarely the problem. Your team is good at the work.

The problem is the space between the work. The quote that sat in someone's inbox for three days. The finished job nobody invoiced until the end of the month. The happy customer nobody asked for a review.

Grab a pen and map one job from first call to final payment. Circle every place it waits on a human to notice something. That is your automation list.

An agent does not replace the person who writes the quote. It makes sure the quote goes out the same afternoon.

posts.title: The offer naming prompt
posts.hook: "Call for a quote" is not an offer.
posts.kicker: Let Claude help you name what you actually sell.
posts.caption:
"Services" and "call for a quote" make a customer do all the work. They have to guess what you do, guess what it costs, and guess whether they are the right fit.

A named package does that work for them. "The Spring Reset: full cleanup, first mow, bed edging, done in one visit." Now they know.

Here is how to get there fast. Tell Claude what you sell, who hires you, and what customers complain about before they call. Ask for three packages with plain names and a one-line "this is for you if."

Then ask it to cut every word a customer would not say. Pick the one that makes you nod. It does not have to be perfect. It has to be clearer than "services."

posts.title: The handoff rule
posts.hook: Give your AI a way out.
posts.kicker: Customers forgive a machine that knows its limits.
posts.caption:
The fastest way to make customers hate your AI is to trap them in it.

We have all been there. "I didn't catch that. Please say billing, support, or sales." Four times.

Every agent I build has a way out. If the caller is upset, if it is an emergency, if the job is big, or if the agent simply is not sure, it says so and hands the call to a person. It tells the caller what happens next: "I'm texting Mike right now, he'll call you back within the hour."

That one move is why customers are comfortable talking to my clients' agents. The AI handles the hundred routine calls. A human handles the one that matters most.

posts.title: The volume trick
posts.hook: Ask for 20. Keep 1.
posts.kicker: The first answer is almost never the best one.
posts.caption:
The biggest mistake people make with AI: asking for one of something and taking it.

The first answer is the average answer. That is what it is built to give you.

So ask for twenty. Twenty headlines, twenty subject lines, twenty names for your fall special. Most will be meh. Two or three will make you stop.

Pick those and ask Claude why they work. Then have it combine the best parts into five new versions. This is where the good stuff shows up.

Last step, and do not skip it: read the finalists out loud. If you would not say it to a customer in your driveway, it is not the one.

posts.title: The 15-minute weekly profile routine
posts.hook: Your Google profile is your real homepage.
posts.kicker: Most customers decide before they ever click your site.
posts.caption:
Here is a hard truth for anyone who spent a lot on a website: a big share of your customers never see it.

They search, they see your Google profile, they read three reviews, and they call. Or they call the next one.

That profile is your homepage now, so treat it like one. Fifteen minutes a week:

Reply to every review within a day, and mention the actual job. "So glad the new deck was ready for your daughter's graduation" does more than "Thanks!"

Post one real photo. Real beats pretty.

Keep your hours and services matching everywhere.

The replies are the part people skip, so that is the part I hand to an agent. It drafts, you approve. Your profile stays alive without eating your evening.

posts.title: The vacation test
posts.hook: Could your business survive a week without you?
posts.kicker: Take the vacation test. On paper first.
posts.caption:
Real question: if you disappeared to Santorini for a week, what would break?

For most owners I know, the answer is "everything," and that is not a badge of honor. It is a single point of failure, and the single point is you.

Grab a notebook and list what would fall apart. The phone. The quotes. The follow-ups. The one supplier who only texts you.

Now circle what truly needs you. Your judgment on a big job. A hard conversation. That is usually two or three things.

Everything else can be written down, handed to a person, or handed to an agent. Build that, and then take the trip. You deserve it, and your business will be better for it.

posts.title: A note to past you
posts.hook: Be kind to the version of you who didn't know yet.
posts.kicker: She did her best with what she had.
posts.caption:
There are business decisions I have made that I would do very differently today. The hire. The price. The project I said yes to when my gut said no.

For a long time I replayed them like a highlight reel of mistakes.

What finally helped was realizing that the version of me who made those calls did not know what I know now. She was working hard with the information she had. She was brave enough to try.

If you are carrying something like that, try this: talk to your past self the way you would talk to a friend who is still learning. Gently. With some humor.

You only see it clearly now because you grew. That deserves a little celebration, not more punishment.

posts.title: Give your agent a personality
posts.hook: Give your AI receptionist a name.
posts.kicker: People remember a name. Nobody remembers "the system."
posts.caption:
Our AI receptionist at Modern Mustard Seed is named Mr. Mustard.

That is on purpose. A name turns a piece of software into a character. Characters get remembered, talked about, and forgiven when they are not perfect.

When you set up a voice agent for your business, give it a name that fits your world. A landscaper's agent sounds different than a dentist's. Write a few lines about its personality: how warm, how quick, how funny.

And have it say up front that it is an AI assistant. Customers do not mind talking to a smart, friendly assistant. They mind being fooled.

posts.title: What early customers gave me
posts.hook: Your first customers are your teachers.
posts.kicker: Every hard one taught you something you use today.
posts.caption:
Every business owner has a few customers from the early days they will never forget.

The one who questioned every line of the invoice. The one who called about everything. And the one who said yes to you when you had nothing to show but a promise.

I used to think of the hard ones as problems. Now I think of them as teachers. Almost everything I do well today, I learned from someone who needed more than I knew how to give at the time.

Here is a small challenge. Think of one early customer who took a chance on you. Send them a short note today. Just thank you.

It will make their day. I promise it will make yours too.

posts.title: Why your mess is marketing
posts.hook: Post the blooper.
posts.kicker: Perfect gets scrolled. Real gets remembered.
posts.caption:
Some of my favorite posts from local businesses are the ones that went slightly wrong.

The contractor who dropped the level in the paint. The baker whose frosting slid off the cake. The dog who photobombed the before-and-after.

Those posts get more love than the polished ones, and it makes sense. Polish says "we are a business." A blooper says "we are people, and we are good at this even on a messy day."

So keep your outtakes. Post one real moment for every few polished ones, and caption it honestly.

You do not need to look perfect to be trusted. You need to look real. Real is a lot more fun, too.

posts.title: Find your one weird thing
posts.hook: Be the weird one in your category.
posts.kicker: Boring is invisible. Different gets remembered.
posts.caption:
Look at the websites of the top five businesses in your trade. I will bet they look almost the same. Blue logo, stock photo handshake, "quality service since 2005."

That sameness is your opportunity.

Pick one thing to be known for that nobody else in your category does. A bright color on your truck. A dog who comes to every job. A thank-you cookie on the counter when you leave. A silly name for your service packages.

Then commit to it everywhere, over and over, until people describe you by it. "Oh, the guys with the pink truck."

You do not need to be louder than your competitors. You just need to be the one they remember.

posts.title: The brainstorm that actually works
posts.hook: Ask Claude for 50 unhinged marketing ideas.
posts.kicker: Then do the one that makes you a little nervous.
posts.caption:
When you ask AI for "marketing ideas," you get the same ten ideas everybody gets. Run a promo. Post consistently. Collect reviews.

Try this instead: "Here is my business, my town, and my customers. Give me 50 marketing ideas. The weirder and more fun the better. Nothing boring."

Somewhere around idea 30, it gets good. A mystery-box giveaway. A contest for the ugliest before photo in town. A tiny parade for your 1,000th customer.

Cross off what does not fit you. Circle the ones that make you laugh. Then do the one that makes you a little nervous.

Fun is not the opposite of professional. Fun is what people actually talk about.
